second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The case is Case No. 3:24-cv-00412-RJC in W.D.N.C., Charlotte Division (RFP caption, CMO, protective order). I downloaded the current W.D.N.C. Local Rules (eff. Dec. 1, 2022, the only local-rules version on the court's page) and read LCvR 26.2. It is headed 'DISCOVERY MATERIAL NOT TO BE FILED UNLESS ORDERED OR NEEDED' and says: 'The parties shall not file any initial disclosures, designations of expert witnesses and their reports, discovery requests or responses thereto, deposition transcripts, or other discovery material unless: (1) directed to do so by the Court; ...'. It says nothing about privilege logs. A text search of the whole local-rules PDF for 'privilege' found only an unrelated physician-patient reference, so W.D.N.C. has no local privilege-log rule. Fed. R. Civ. P. 26(b)(5)(A) alone governs.

citations.authority: Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act
citations.citation_as_written: Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act
citations.cited_for: Dissolution to be carried out in accordance with applicable provisions

first_check.correct_citation: Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act, 6 Del. C. ch. 17 (§ 17-101 et seq.)
first_check.explanation: The Act exists: 6 Del. C. § 17-1102 gives it that short title. It governs only Delaware limited partnerships, though. The joint venture here is called a 'Delaware joint venture entity' that files a 'certificate of formation', which is limited-liability-company terminology, and nothing says it is a limited partnership. So the Act's fit is doubtful, but the clause only invokes 'applicable provisions', so it is not plainly wrong. A related defect: the companion 'Delaware Uniform Partnership Law' is not an official name. Delaware's partnership statute is the 'Delaware Revised Uniform Partnership Act' (6 Del. C. ch. 15). The citation also gives no chapter number.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: § 17-1102: "This chapter may be cited as the 'Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act.'"; Chapter 15 heading: "CHAPTER 15. Delaware Revised Uniform Partnership Act"

citations.cited_for: Dissolution of the JV governed by applicable provisions
citations.context: the Delaware Revised Uniform Limited Partnership Act, the Delaware Uniform Partnership Law, and other applicable provisions of Delaware law governing the dissolution of joint ventures

first_check.correct_citation: Delaware Revised Uniform Partnership Act, 6 Del. C. § 15-101 et seq. (dissolution at § 15-801 et seq.); the former Delaware Uniform Partnership Law was 6 Del. C. § 1501 et seq.
first_check.explanation: A 'Delaware Uniform Partnership Law' did exist: it was the former 6 Del. C. § 1501 et seq. The Delaware Revised Uniform Partnership Act (6 Del. C. ch. 15) replaced it. Today it survives only as a historical reference point, for example in § 17-403(b) ('in effect on July 11, 1999'). The statute that now governs dissolution of a Delaware general partnership or joint venture is DRUPA, Subchapter VIII (§ 15-801 et seq.). The agreement names a superseded statute as current governing law. The general proposition still holds, because the clause also invokes 'other applicable provisions of Delaware law', but the statute name is outdated.
first_check.evidence_excerpt: § 17-403(b): "a general partner of a limited partnership has the liabilities of a partner in a partnership that is governed by the Delaware Uniform Partnership Law in effect on July 11, 1999 (6 Del. C. § 1501 et seq.)"

second_check.explanation: The finding holds. The 'Delaware Uniform Partnership Law' was a real statute (former 6 Del. C. § 1501 et seq.), but it was repealed long before this 2019 JV and its dissolution. DRUPA § 15-1205 states the prior Delaware Uniform Partnership Law (§§ 1501-1553) was repealed effective January 1, 2002, except as to limited partnerships. § 15-1206(b) says that from January 1, 2002, 'this chapter governs all partnerships.' Today the old statute is mentioned only as a historical benchmark in § 17-403(b): 'governed by the Delaware Uniform Partnership Law in effect on July 11, 1999 (6 Del. C. § 1501 et seq.)'. The general reference to 'other applicable provisions of Delaware law' still covers DRUPA, so the defect is a superseded statute name, not a fabrication.

citations.cited_for: Permits deferral of contention interrogatories until after discovery is substantially complete; RFP No. 41 as disguised contention interrogatory

first_check.explanation: Rule 33(a)(2) says contention interrogatories are not objectionable as such, but the court may order that they need not be answered until designated discovery is complete, until a pretrial conference, or until some other time. That supports deferring contention discovery. The parenthetical is loose in two ways. Deferral is a discretionary court order, not something the rule grants by itself, and the rule says 'designated discovery is complete,' not 'substantially complete.' Also, the rule governs interrogatories, so applying it to RFP No. 41 is an analogy, which the rubric's 'otherwise articulates' alternative allows.

The rule does not fix when the order must be obtained, but getting it before production begins is a reasonable application of the rule, and the rubric presents it as advice rather than as a requirement of the rule.

Pointing to the volume of about 950,000 documents (where inadvertent production is more likely) is a fact-specific argument that fits the rule's purpose.
